---
title: "Centering and scaling"
---

The [PHOIBLE matrix](data-matrices.qmd) represents inventory records in rows and retained segment listings in columns. Every column uses the same binary database-listing unit, but the columns differ in how often a segment is listed. Centering changes each column's origin. Standardization would additionally change its unit and, for binary data, its weight in the factorization.

## Centering changes the origin

For column $j$, the training mean is

$$
\widehat\mu_j
=
\frac{1}{n_{\mathcal T}}
\sum_{i\in\mathcal T}x_{ij}.
$$

Because $x_{ij}$ is binary here, $\widehat\mu_j$ is the training proportion of inventory records that list segment $j$. The centered entry is

$$
z_{ij}=x_{ij}-\widehat\mu_j,
$$

and the complete centered training matrix is

$$
\mathbf Z_{\mathcal T}
=
\mathbf X_{\mathcal T}
-
\mathbf 1_{n_{\mathcal T}}\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{\mathsf T}.
$$

Every column of $\mathbf Z_{\mathcal T}$ has mean zero. Centering does not alter differences between inventory records. It changes the reference point from “not listed” to the observed training prevalence.

## Scaling changes the unit

The sample standard deviation of column $j$ is

$$
s_j
=
\sqrt{
\frac{1}{n_{\mathcal T}-1}
\sum_{i\in\mathcal T}
(x_{ij}-\widehat\mu_j)^2
}.
$$

Collecting these values on the diagonal of $\mathbf S$, the standardized matrix is

$$
\widetilde{\mathbf Z}_{\mathcal T}
=
\mathbf Z_{\mathcal T}\mathbf S^{-1},
$$

or, cell by cell,

$$
\widetilde z_{ij}
=
\frac{x_{ij}-\widehat\mu_j}{s_j}.
$$

The transformation makes each nonconstant training column have mean zero and sample standard deviation one. Thus it gives every segment column the same variance before factorization.

## Computing the PHOIBLE coordinate systems

This page independently reconstructs the row selection, split, and training-only column set introduced on the [previous page](data-matrices.qmd).

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

phoible <- readRDS("data/phoible/phoible-pilot.rds")

select_one <- function(inventories, seed = 20260827L) {
  inventories <- inventories[
    order(inventories$glottocode, as.integer(inventories$inventory_id)),
  ]
  groups <- split(seq_len(nrow(inventories)), inventories$glottocode)
  RNGkind(sample.kind = "Rejection")
  set.seed(seed)
  rows <- vapply(groups, function(x) x[[sample.int(length(x), 1L)]], integer(1))
  inventories[unname(rows), ]
}

split_by_area <- function(selected, seed = 20261018L) {
  area <- selected$macroarea
  area[is.na(area) | area == ""] <- "Unclassified"
  answer <- rep(NA_character_, nrow(selected))
  set.seed(seed)
  for (name in sort(unique(area))) {
    index <- sample(which(area == name))
    n_holdout <- floor(0.15 * length(index))
    answer[index[seq_len(n_holdout)]] <- "validation"
    answer[index[n_holdout + seq_len(n_holdout)]] <- "test"
    answer[index[is.na(answer[index])]] <- "training"
  }
  answer
}

selected <- select_one(phoible$inventories)
selected$split <- split_by_area(selected)
training_rows <- which(selected$split == "training")

memberships <- merge(
  phoible$memberships,
  selected[c("inventory_id", "glottocode")],
  by = c("inventory_id", "glottocode")
)
frequency <- table(
  memberships$segment_id[memberships$glottocode %in%
    selected$glottocode[training_rows]]
)
column_ids <- sort(names(frequency)[frequency >= 20L])
X <- matrix(
  0,
  nrow = nrow(selected),
  ncol = length(column_ids),
  dimnames = list(selected$glottocode, column_ids)
)
retained <- memberships[memberships$segment_id %in% column_ids, ]
X[cbind(
  match(retained$glottocode, rownames(X)),
  match(retained$segment_id, colnames(X))
)] <- 1

training_mean <- colMeans(X[training_rows, , drop = FALSE])
training_sd <- apply(X[training_rows, , drop = FALSE], 2, sd)
Z <- sweep(X[training_rows, , drop = FALSE], 2, training_mean, "-")
Z_standardized <- sweep(Z, 2, training_sd, "/")

c(
  largest_absolute_centered_mean = max(abs(colMeans(Z))),
  largest_standardized_sd_error = max(abs(apply(Z_standardized, 2, sd) - 1))
)
```

The training set contains `r nrow(Z)` inventory records and `r ncol(Z)` retained segments. No retained column is constant because the training-frequency rule removes segments with too few listings.

## The empirical weighting decision

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.6

transformation <- data.frame(
  prevalence = training_mean,
  multiplier = 1 / training_sd
)

prevalence_plot <- ggplot(transformation, aes(x = prevalence)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 24, fill = "grey35", color = "white") + # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
  labs(x = "Training listing proportion", y = "Segment columns") +
  theme_classic()

multiplier_plot <- ggplot(transformation, aes(x = multiplier)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 24, fill = "grey35", color = "white") + # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
  labs(x = "Standardization multiplier (1 / s)", y = "Segment columns") +
  theme_classic()

if (requireNamespace("patchwork", quietly = TRUE)) {
  prevalence_plot + multiplier_plot
} else {
  prevalence_plot
  multiplier_plot
}
```

The least variable retained column would be multiplied by `r round(max(transformation$multiplier), 2)`, whereas the most variable would be multiplied by `r round(min(transformation$multiplier), 2)`. Standardization would thus assign relatively greater weight to rare segment listings. That weighting may be useful for some questions, but it is not neutral.

The primary PHOIBLE analysis centers without variance standardization. Every column already shares the same listing unit, and the analysis lets common patterns contribute their observed variance. This choice does not claim that common segments are linguistically more important. It defines the numerical target of this factorization.

## Applying a fitted transformation

Means and scales used for evaluation must come from training data. For a new matrix $\mathbf X_{\mathrm{new}}$, the fixed transformation is

$$
\mathbf Z_{\mathrm{new}}
=
(\mathbf X_{\mathrm{new}}-
\mathbf 1\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}^{\mathsf T})
\mathbf S^{-1}.
$$

In R, that operation is:

```{r}
X_new <- X[selected$split == "validation", , drop = FALSE]
X_new_centered <- sweep(X_new, 2, training_mean, "-")
X_new_standardized <- sweep(X_new_centered, 2, training_sd, "/")
```

Recomputing the means or standard deviations on validation rows would let held-out records change their own coordinate system. That is [leakage through preprocessing](../model-criticism-and-prediction/training-and-test-data.qmd#leakage-through-preprocessing).
